readerTitle: The decision you'll still think about in ten years
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계 대행 사무소, 철물점) + 실제 연구 (Gilovich & Medvec 1995, Gilbert 외 2004)
insight: 드물고 큰 결정은 내년 숫자가 아니라 먼 미래의 내가 어느 쪽을 더 후회할지로 비교하고, 감당할 수 있는 손실 범위 안에서 실행한다.
misconception: 후회를 줄이려면 아무것도 바꾸지 않고 안전한 쪽에 머무는 것이 낫다. 또는 반대로, 후회 최소화는 무조건 크게 저지르라는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Gilovich, T. & Medvec, V. H. (1995). The experience of regret: What, when, and why. Psychological Review, 102(2), 379–395.
Gilbert, D. T., Morewedge, C. K., Risen, J. L. & Wilson, T. D. (2004). Looking forward to looking backward: The misprediction of regret. Psychological Science, 15(5), 346–350.
Jeff Bezos, interview with the Academy of Achievement (2001), describing the 'regret minimization framework'

factChecks.note: Gilovich & Medvec(1995)의 핵심 결론: 단기적으로는 한 일(행동)을 더 후회하고, 장기적으로는 하지 않은 일(비행동)을 더 후회한다. 카드에는 수치 없이 방향만 적었습니다. 원문 요약과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
Gilbert 외(2004): 사람들은 결과가 나쁠 때 느낄 후회의 강도를 실제보다 크게 예측한다. 카드에는 일반적 결론만 적었습니다.
Bezos가 'regret minimization framework'라는 표현을 쓴 출처(2001년 Academy of Achievement 인터뷰 등)를 확인하세요. 상세 일화는 THK-09-09에서 다루므로 여기서는 이름의 유래만 한 문장으로 언급했습니다.
회계 사무소와 철물점 사례, 금액은 모두 설명용 가상 설정입니다.

cards.title: The decision you'll still think about in ten years
body: Lena runs a six-person bookkeeping firm. It's steady. Clients pay on time.
For three years she has wanted to specialize in restaurants, the clients she understands best. Every January she runs the numbers, and every January the idea waits one more year.

image.label: Business owner at a desk late at night, an old note pinned above
image.brief: 밤늦은 작은 사무실. 책상 앞의 여성 사업가가 노트북 스프레드시트를 보고 있고, 벽에 빛바랜 메모 "Restaurants?"가 세 장 겹쳐 붙어 있음(해마다 붙인 느낌). 따뜻하고 차분한 일러스트. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Lena make this call?
body: A restaurant owners' association offers her a partner slot. Taking it means about six months of focus and letting go of a few general clients. The forecast says it might pay off, or might not.

options.text: Wait another year until the forecast is clearer
options.feedback: Waiting feels free, but it has quietly cost her three years already. The forecast rarely gets clearer, and the offer may not come back.

options.text: Decide on next year's expected revenue alone
options.feedback: The numbers matter, but a one-year view can't see what this choice means for the firm she wants to run in ten years.

options.text: Picture herself ten years out and ask which choice she'd regret more, then limit how much she could lose
options.feedback: This weighs the long view and still protects the business. It's the idea in this lesson.

cards.title: The spreadsheet answers a different question.
body: Lena's forecast compares two outcomes next year. Both look similar, so staying put always wins. Staying put feels safe.
But she isn't really choosing between two revenue figures. She's choosing between two stories she'll tell about her firm later: *I tried it* or *I never found out*.
Only one of those stories keeps bothering her every January.

cards.title: Regret minimization
body: **Regret minimization** means picturing yourself far in the future, looking back, and asking which choice you'd regret more.
Jeff Bezos popularized the name when describing his own career choice. The idea is simple: for big, rare decisions, the long-term view of regret is a better guide than short-term comfort.

image.label: Person today and an older self looking back along a path
image.brief: 왼쪽에 갈림길 앞에 선 현재의 사람, 오른쪽 끝에 같은 사람의 나이 든 모습이 뒤돌아보는 장면. 두 갈래 길 중 한쪽은 "Tried", 다른 쪽은 "Never found out" 표지판. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.softwareNote: A founder deciding whether to quit a stable job, or to rebuild a product around a new kind of user, faces the same question. The quarterly numbers rarely settle it; the ten-year view often does.

cards.title: Over time, we regret what we didn't do.
body: Psychologists Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec studied what people regret. In the short term, people regret **actions** more, the mistake they made last week.
Looking back over years, the pattern flips. People regret **inactions** more: the chance not taken, the idea never tested.
So a choice that feels safe today can become the heaviest regret later. Regret minimization tries to account for that shift before you decide.

cards.title: Use it for rare, big, hard-to-undo choices.
list: Starting, selling or reshaping a business
Entering a new market or dropping an old one
Hiring a partner or parting with one
cards.callout: For daily calls like pricing a quote or ordering stock, the ten-year lens is overkill. Ordinary numbers do the job.
cards.softwareNote: Choosing a button color doesn't need it. Choosing whether to rebuild your product for a new market might.

cards.title: Regret doesn't pay the rent.
body: Research by Daniel Gilbert and colleagues found that people tend to overestimate how much regret they'll feel when things go wrong. Imagined regret is a rough guide, not a precise one.

And avoiding the regret of not trying can push you into a bet that sinks the business. The method works best paired with a limit: **try the bold option, but only in a size you can survive** if it fails.

cards.title: Now it's a hardware store.
body: Sam runs his family's hardware store. He's sure a second store in a growing town nearby would work, and he'd regret never trying. The bank will lend if he puts up the original store as security.

options.text: Sign the loan and open a full store. Regret says go big
options.feedback: He avoids the regret of not trying, but one bad year could cost him both stores. That's a regret he'd feel far longer.

options.text: Test with a small, short-lease shop or a delivery service to that town first
options.feedback: He answers the question he'd regret not asking, while keeping the original store safe. If it works, he can scale up.

options.text: Skip it. The first store is enough
options.feedback: It protects what he has, but leaves the question open for years. That kind of unanswered question is what people tend to regret most.

cards.title: Ask what you'll regret, then make the bet survivable.
body: For big, rare choices, picture yourself ten years out. Pick the path you'd regret skipping, in a size you can afford to lose.
**Try it today:** write down one idea you've postponed for over a year. Ask which you'd regret more in ten years, and what the smallest safe test would be.
